## Lab 07 Assignment - Group 20

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)  # devtools::install_github("tidymodels/broom")
library(cowplot)
```

```{r}
biopsy <- read_csv("https://wilkelab.org/classes/SDS348/data_sets/biopsy.csv")
```

```{r}
pca_fit <- biopsy %>% 
  select(where(is.numeric)) %>% # retain only numeric columns
  prcomp(scale = TRUE) # do PCA on scaled data

pca_fit
```

```{r}
pca_fit <- biopsy %>% 
  select(where(is.numeric)) %>% # retain only numeric columns
  scale() %>% # scale data
  prcomp() # do PCA

pca_fit
```

### Correlation Matrix of the Biopsy Variables

Before running PCA, visualizing the correlation matrix of the variables, using the ggcorrplot package, will check if they are related to each other. Only the lower triangle is shown because the matrix is symmetric and similar variables are grouped together.

```{r}
library(ggcorrplot)

biopsy_data <- biopsy |> 
  select(where(is.numeric))
corr_matrix <- cor(biopsy_data)
ggcorrplot(corr_matrix,
           hc.order = TRUE,
           type = "lower",
           lab = TRUE,
           lab_size = 3, 
           title = "Correlation Between the Biopsy Variables",
           legend.title = "Correlation") +
  labs(caption = "Data from the Wisconsin Breast Cancer Database") 
```

### **Analysis**

All correlations are positive, with the strongest one between uniform cell size and uniform cell shape. This shows that these two variables carry almost the same information. Mitoses shows the weakest correlations with the other variables. This confirms that PCA is a suitable method for this data.
